title: Lighthouses of California
subtitle: Every light station, fog signal, and lightship station, 1854–1939
abstract: Every documented light station on the California coast and inside San Francisco Bay — from the first federal cohort of 1854 to the last stations built before the Second World War — together with the fog-signal stations, the minor bay beacons, and the two lightship stations that held position where no tower could stand. Each pin carries the station's first lighting, its lens, its rebuildings, its automation and fate, and, where the record allows, the words of the Light-House Board itself: this map's primary layer is 173 passages quoted from the Board's annual reports, located in the Treasury's printed volumes and cited to report year and page. Those reports correct the received story in places. The Board never called Alcatraz the first lighthouse on the Pacific coast; its own printed Light List of 1858 gives both Alcatraz and Point Pinos as built in 1854 and does not rank them. Mare Island's fog bell came from Point Bonita, not Cape Mendocino. And the Board located Mare Island's own tower at the island's "southern end" in 1872 and its "extreme eastern end" in 1874 — so that pin, like three others whose stations are gone and whose positions were never published, is an area estimate with its derivation stated in the popup rather than a false precision. Layers are the eras of building; filters cut by station type, present condition, and region.
legend_note: Layers are eras of establishment. Pin size marks the kind of aid (light station, lightship station, fog signal, minor beacon). Dashed pins are area estimates — four vanished stations whose positions were never published are derived from period descriptions, with the derivation given in the popup.

features.name: St. George Reef Light Station

date.display: First exhibited 20 October 1892

features.summary: Long described in the lighthouse literature as the most expensive American lighthouse ever built, St. George Reef took eight working seasons (1883-1891) to raise on a wave-swept rock six miles off Point St. George, using 1,339 dressed granite blocks quarried near the Mad River. Its first-order flashing lens went into service in 1892 and warned shipping off the reef that had claimed the Brother Jonathan in 1865. The Coast Guard disestablished the station in May 1975 in favor of a buoy; the tower still stands and again shows a private light.
facts: First-order lens installed August 1892; station in operation by October 1892 (NRHP nomination 93001373, which quotes the 1892 Annual Report of the Light-House Board; the nomination dates a keeper's death 17 Oct 1893 'hardly a year after the station began operation'). The Board's report for 1893 (p. 167) describes the lens reaching the station in August and the light going into service that October; 20 October 1892 is the day given in the lighthouse literature.

Single granite tower on Northwest Seal Rock, built 1883-1891/92 on an elliptical concrete-and-granite pier; keepers withdrawn and station disestablished 13 May 1975 (nomination); relit as a restored private aid (Light List 2025, 'Restored historic light').
First-order Fresnel, 1892, flashing alternately red and white (NRHP nomination; USCG Historian's Office). Lens removed 1975 to the Del Norte County Historical Society museum (nomination).

Marks the offshore reef where the steamer Brother Jonathan sank in 1865; the USCG Historian's Office narrative states the light 'marks the site of the tragic sinking of the steamer Brother Jonathan.' Land reserved by President Andrew Johnson after a May 1866 Light-House Board draft; construction 1883-1891 under Capt. A.H. Payson and then A. Ballantyne, total cost about $704,634-$726,000 (nomination quoting the 1892 Annual Report).
Never conventionally automated on station; USCG table marks 'automated' without a year. Disestablished 13 May 1975 and replaced by a lighted buoy.
13 May 1975 (NRHP nomination); relit as a private aid in the 2000s-2010s (Light List 2025 carries it as LLNR 561, Fl W 12s, 'Restored historic light'; relight year 2012 is tertiary only).

Standing; owned by Del Norte County per USCG page; maintained by the St. George Reef Lighthouse Preservation Society (tertiary; not independently verified). First-order lens displayed at Del Norte County Historical Society, Crescent City.
Listed 1993-12-09, ref 93001373, under Light Stations of California MPS (NRIS dataset 2026-05-22).

On 17 October 1893, about a year after operations began, the first assistant keeper lost his life at the station (NRHP nomination); the USCG narrative adds that several men were injured or killed over the years transferring to the rock by small boat, and describes an 1923 storm that tore the donkey-engine house from its foundation 70 feet above the water.
US Coast Guard Light List Vol. VI 2025, LLNR 561 (41-50-14.000N 124-22-32.000W); cross-checked against corrected UTM 10/385800/4632400 in NRHP nomination 93001373

quotes.text: 824. St. George Reef, Northwest Seal Rock, seacoast of California.—By the middle of the first month of the fiscal year all the stone required for the completion of this work was quarried and cut, when the available funds not being sufficient to warrant resumption of construction, all work was shut down, the plant stored at the stone yard, and that place left in charge of a watchman. During the year the specifications and drawings for the metalwork for the tower were prepared and contract was made with the Phoenix Iron Company of Trenton, N. J., for its construction. By the end of the fiscal year it was completed and on its way to San Francisco. An item in the general deficiency act approved September 30, 1890, appropriated $81,000 for the completion of this station.
quotes.cite: Annual Report of the Light-House Board (GPO), 1891, p. pp. 160–161 (both leaves image-verified)

quotes.text: 862. St. George Reef, Northwest Seal Rock, seacoast of California.—There will be found in an appendix to this volume an interesting description by Mr. A. Ballantyne, superintendent of construction of the Northwest Seal Rock Light-Station, California, of the early history, annual progress, and many incidents and facts connected with this work. There have been prepared from the office records, also, tabulated statements showing in detail the cost of its different parts. The work was commenced in 1883 and it was completed in 1891. The long time required for its construction and completion, together with the incidental expenses, were due, in a great measure, to inadequate appropriations.

quotes.text: 888. St. George Reef, Pacific Ocean, on Northwest Seal Rock, St. George Reef, California.—This station was completed last year, except the lens, which had not then been received. features.name: Battery Point Light (Crescent City)

date.display: First exhibited 10 December 1856 (USC&GS Pacific Coast Pilot, 4th ed. 1889: 'first exhibit

features.summary: Battery Point is one of the survivors of California's first generation of lighthouses: a brick tower rising through a granite Cape Cod dwelling on a tidal islet at Crescent City, first exhibited 10 December 1856. Automated in 1953 and dark from 1965, it was relit as a private aid on 10 December 1982 and now operates as a county museum still showing a light.
facts: First exhibited 10 December 1856 (USC&GS Pacific Coast Pilot, 4th ed. 1889: 'first exhibited on the 10th of December, 1856'; the same passage notes it was not shown for a period beginning April 1860).

1856 Cape Cod-type dwelling with integral tower on Battery Point islet, one of the first West Coast lighthouses; still the original structure. Automatic light installed July 1953; leased to Del Norte County; light deactivated 1965-1982 (USCG); relit as a private aid 10 December 1982 (NRHP nomination).

One of the first cohort of Pacific coast lighthouses authorized in the early 1850s to serve the gold-rush coastal trade; Crescent City was one of only two real harbors (with Humboldt Bay) on the redwood north coast (Bookwalter, Light Stations of California MPS, 1989).
1965-1982 (USCG table); relit 10 December 1982 as a private aid (nomination). Active today as LLNR 555, Fl W 30s, 'Restored historic light.'
Standing; museum operated with Del Norte County (county lease from 1953 per USCG); tidal-island access.
Listed 1983-09-15 as 'Cresent City Lighthouse' [sic], ref 83001177 (NRIS dataset).

quotes.text: 457. Crescent City, sea-coast of California. — This station is in a dilapidated condition, and should be rebuilt if the light is to be continued. The entire wood-work of the keeper's stone dwelling must be removed. The ends of many of the lower floor-timbers are entirely gone, and the floor is held up by shores. features.name: Trinidad Head Light Station

date.display: 1871 (USC&GS Coast Pilot 1889: 'first exhibited in 1871'; NRHP nomination 91001098 and USC

features.summary: A squat brick tower of 1871 whose modest height — 18 feet from ground line to focal plane, in the Board's own figure — is multiplied by Trinidad Head's 196-foot cliff, this light covered the crowded lumber-schooner harbor at Trinidad. It keeps its original station arrangement minus the razed Victorian dwelling, and its 1871 lens survives in a replica tower in town. It remains an active Coast Guard aid, automated in 1974.
facts: 1871 (USC&GS Coast Pilot 1889: 'first exhibited in 1871'; NRHP nomination 91001098 and USCG concur on 1871; and the Board's own report for 1872 (p. 547) dates the first lighting to the night of 1 December 1871).

1871 square pyramidal brick tower, still standing and basically unchanged; 1898 bell house with 4,000-lb fog bell; original Victorian dwelling razed late 1960s for a Coast Guard triplex (USCG). Original 4th-order lens removed 1947 and installed 1948-49 in a memorial replica tower in the town of Trinidad (USCG; NRHP nomination says the original lens was installed in the replica in 1948).
Fourth-order Fresnel, 1871; replaced 1947 by a 375 mm optic (USCG).

Served Trinidad Harbor and the north-coast lumber trade; the nomination's significance statement runs from 1871 under commerce, transportation and maritime history, within the doghole-port economy described in the Light Stations of California MPS.
Never; active USCG aid (Light List 2025, Oc W 4s, HORN).
Standing; active aid with Coast Guard housing on the head; original lens and bell displayed at the town's memorial lighthouse.
Listed 1991-09-03, ref 91001098, Light Stations of California MPS (NRIS).

In 1913 the keeper reported a freak wave that struck the 196-foot headland: "The sea shot up the face of the bluff and over it, until the solid sea seemed to me to be on a level with where I stood in the lantern... The whole point between the tower and the bluff was buried in water" (quoted on the USCG Historian's Office page).

features.name: Table Bluff Light Station

date.display: 1892 (USCG Historian's Office: 'In 1892 the Lighthouse Service constructed a light station

features.summary: Table Bluff took over Humboldt Bay's seacoast light in 1892 from the failing North Spit station, placing a Stick-style dwelling-tower on the high bluff south of the bay. The Navy added a radio station in 1906 and the site swelled with beach-patrol and radio-compass functions in WWII, after which most of the original complex was demolished. Automated in 1953, the light was discontinued in the 1970s and the property sold.
facts: 1892 (USCG Historian's Office: "In 1892 the Lighthouse Service constructed a light station on Table Bluff"; NPS inventory: 'TABLE BLUFF LIGHT (1892)'). The day, 31 October 1892, follows the Board's report for 1893.

1892 Stick-style keeper's dwelling with attached square wooden tower (near-twin of San Luis Obispo), duplex quarters and fog-signal building; most station buildings razed during and after WWII, leaving the tower and fog-signal building; the quarters portion of the lighthouse itself was razed leaving only the tower (USCG). The MPS context groups its fanciful Stick-style plans with San Luis Obispo and Ballast Point.

Fourth-order rotating Fresnel; in 1953 replaced by a fixed smaller lens and the 4th-order optic shipped to Old Point Loma for museum display; the later lens went to the Smithsonian on discontinuation (USCG; the page gives the replacement lens inconsistently as '3 1/2 order' and '2 1/2 order').

Replaced the 1856 Humboldt Harbor light on the sinking, low North Spit, 'for many years... criticized as being too low' (USCG); the 1889 Coast Pilot already records that 'it has been proposed to remove the Humboldt Light-house to this bluff.'
1953; fog signal discontinued the same year (USCG).
1975 per the USCG narrative ("In 1975 the light was discontinued and the property transferred to GSA and sold"); the same page's data table says deactivated 1961 - conflict noted.
Station property sold; tower reportedly relocated to Woodley Island, Eureka, in the 1980s (tertiary, not verified in located records).
Not found in the NRIS listed-properties dataset (2026-05-22); apparently never listed.

quotes.text: 821. Humboldt, entrance to Humboldt Bay, California.—Congress at its last session appropriated $25,000 for the reestablishment of this station on a new site. The Light-House Board having decided that the best interests of navigation would be subserved by locating the new station on Table Bluff, a point about 4 miles south of the present light, the inspector and engineer of this district visited the place on May 8, 1891, and selected a site for the station. The owner of the selected land refused to sell for less than $5,000 for about 10 acres of land and the right of way for a road from the county road to the proposed station. This price was deemed exorbitant, and measures were initiated to acquire title by condemnation.
quotes.cite: Annual Report of the Light-House Board (GPO), 1891, p. p. 160 (image-verified)

quotes.text: 859. Humboldt, entrance to Humboldt Bay, California.—The suit brought to obtain, by condemnation, title to the land needed for the reestablishment of this station on Table Bluff was withdrawn and a compromise was made with the owner whereby the United States secured for $2,220 some 10 acres of land, together with the right to take water from an adjacent spring.
quotes.cite: Annual Report of the Light-House Board (GPO), 1892, p. p. 186 (OCR only; NOT image-verified)

quotes.text: 885. Humboldt, near the western edge of Table Bluff, entrance to Humboldt Bay, California.—The reestablishment of this station on the new site at Table Bluff, commenced last year, was continued until October 5, 1892, when it was satisfactorily completed. The lens and one fog-signal boiler were kept at the old station until October 31, the date set for starting the new station. On October 31, the light was exhibited from the new station and the old station was abandoned. The new station on Table Bluff consists of a keeper's dwelling and tower combined, a double dwelling for the assistant keepers, a fog-signal building containing two boilers and engines and a coal shed.
quotes.cite: Annual Report of the Light-House Board (GPO), 1893, p. pp. 166–167 (both leaves image-verified)

features.name: Humboldt Harbor Light (1856)

date.display: First exhibited 20 December 1856 (USC&GS Pacific Coast Pilot, 4th ed. 1889: 'The Light was

features.summary: Lit on 20 December 1856, the Humboldt Harbor light was a brick Cape Cod dwelling-tower planted on the low, unstable North Spit of Humboldt Bay. Sited too low and plagued by fog and settling ground, it was criticized for decades; the Coast Survey was already reporting a proposal to move the light to Table Bluff in 1889, and the 1892 Table Bluff station superseded it.
facts: First exhibited 20 December 1856 (USC&GS Pacific Coast Pilot, 4th ed. 1889: "The Light was first exhibited on December 20, 1856").

1856 one-and-a-half-story brick keeper's dwelling with a conical tower rising 21 feet above the roof, plastered and painted white (Coast Pilot 1889). Superseded by Table Bluff in 1892; the MPS context cites it as the type-case of a Cape Cod design failing 'when constructed on the sinking sands of Humboldt Bay.'

Fourth-order Fresnel, fixed white (Coast Pilot 1889). The third-order lens originally intended for Humboldt Harbor was diverted to Old Point Loma in 1855 (USCG Historian's Office, Old Point Loma entry).

Humboldt Bay was one of the two harbors of the redwood coast and the outlet of its lumber trade; one of the first cohort of Pacific lighthouses funded in the early 1850s (MPS context; Coast Pilot 1889 notes the excessive fog at the site).
1892, when Table Bluff was established (USCG Table Bluff entry).
Abandoned after 1892; ruins later lost (final demolition/collapse date not verified in located sources).

No published coordinate located. The 1889 Coast Pilot places it 'on the North Spit or Peninsula, three-quarters of a mile north of the entrance to the bay and about midway between the bay and the sea-shores.'

features.name: Cape Mendocino Light Station

date.display: First exhibited 1 December 1868 (Coast Pilot 1889: 'The Light was first exhibited December

features.summary: Lit on 1 December 1868, Cape Mendocino's prefabricated cast-iron tower stood 422 feet above the Pacific on the state's westernmost cape, its first-order flash marking the great turn of the coast. Automated in 1951 and abandoned by the 1970s, the little tower was dismantled in 1998 and rebuilt at Shelter Cove, while its lens has sat in Ferndale since 1948.
facts: First exhibited 1 December 1868 (Coast Pilot 1889: "The Light was first exhibited December 1, 1868"; USCG concurs: 'activated on December 1, 1868').

1868 prefabricated 16-sided cast-iron pyramidal tower, 43 ft, one of the highest lights in the U.S. at 422 ft above the sea; the MPS groups its iron-plate prefabrication with Point Reyes. Automated 1951; abandoned 1970s; tower dismantled and re-erected 1998 at Mal Coombs Park, Shelter Cove (USCG).
First-order Fresnel, revolving (Coast Pilot 1889; USCG). Lens moved 1948 to a replica tower at the Humboldt County Fairgrounds, Ferndale (USCG).

Cape Mendocino is the westernmost turning point of the California coast and its most prominent seamark for coastwise traffic; a first-order coastal light of the post-Civil War expansion (MPS context; Coast Pilot describes it as the abrupt termination of a mountainous ridge).
Station abandoned in the 1970s (USCG table: 'Deactivated: 1970s'); a minor light on the site continued later per tertiary sources (Wikipedia infobox gives 2013), not verified.
Tower preserved at Shelter Cove (Cape Mendocino Lighthouse Preservation Society, per USCG); lens at Ferndale fairgrounds.

features.name: Punta Gorda Light Station

date.display: 15 January 1912: 'The fog-signal... went into operation on June 22, 1911

features.summary: The 'Alcatraz of lighthouses' on the Lost Coast was built after the Columbia disaster of 1907 capped a dozen years of wrecks below Cape Mendocino; its fog sirens sounded from June 1911 and the fourth-order light first shone on 15 January 1912. Nearly roadless its whole working life, the station was extinguished on 15 February 1951, and only the small concrete lighthouse and oil house survived the BLM's burn of the abandoned quarters.
facts: 15 January 1912: 'The fog-signal... went into operation on June 22, 1911; and a half a year later, on January 15, 1912, the station's light shown for the first time' (NRHP nomination 76000483).

Built 1910-11: reinforced-concrete light building (a squat two-story block), concrete oil house, wooden fog-signal building, three two-story frame keepers' dwellings, shops and barn strung along the beach bench (nomination). Light extinguished 15 February 1951; BLM burned all buildings except the lighthouse and oil house after 1960s squatting (nomination; USCG).

Fourth-order lens with incandescent oil-vapor lamp, focal plane 75 ft, visible 14 miles; electric lamp only from the 1940s (nomination). USCG table calls it a 'fourth order, bulls eye 1912.' Whereabouts of the lens unknown (USCG).

Ten ships sank or stranded near Punta Gorda 1895-1907, ending with the Columbia, which collided with a lumber schooner on 12 July 1907 with 77 lives lost; 'this disaster was undoubtedly the impetus,' and Congress appropriated $60,000 in 1908 (nomination). The steamer St. Paul's 1905 boiler still lay a few hundred feet from the construction site.
Unknown/none - USCG marks automation 'UNK'; the station was simply discontinued.

Lighthouse and oil house stand on the remote Lost Coast; transferred to BLM 16 January 1963 (nomination). The 2016 USCG page instead says California Dept. of Parks and Recreation - conflict unresolved (the site is commonly described as BLM King Range NCA).
Listed 1976-09-01, ref 76000483 (NRIS dataset serial; ArcGIS layer lacks it).

One of the loneliest posts in the district: supplies came by boat until 1915 and afterward by horse and wagon from Petrolia, ten and a half miles away, with creeks cutting the route off for seven months a year (nomination). After closure, squatters occupied the quarters until BLM evicted them and burned every building but the concrete pair (USCG).

features.summary: Point Arena's first-order light of 1 May 1870 stood only 36 years before the 1906 San Andreas rupture, whose trace passes just offshore, shattered the brick tower. Its 1908 replacement, a slim reinforced-concrete shaft raised by a San Francisco chimney firm, was the first reinforced-concrete lighthouse in California, per its National Register nomination. Marked the prominent Point Arena headland and its dangerous outlying reef for the coastwise lumber and passenger trade north of San Francisco (Coast Pilot 1889 landfall description; MPS context).

features.name: Point Reyes Light Station

date.display: First exhibited 1 December 1870 (Coast Pilot 1889: first-order lens 'first exhibited Decem

features.summary: Set into the cliff-face 294 feet above the surf because fog smothers the 600-foot headland above, Point Reyes first showed its first-order flash on 1 December 1870. Its iron-plate tower and clockwork lens served through a century of gales before automation in 1975, and the station now anchors the maritime story of Point Reyes National Seashore.
facts: First exhibited 1 December 1870 (Coast Pilot 1889: first-order lens 'first exhibited December 1, 1870').

1870 sixteen-sided forged-iron-plate tower bolted to rock 294 ft above the sea, reached by 304 steps from the headland (USCG 1962 pamphlet quote); fog-signal building, engine room and later quarters above. A modern automated beacon took over in 1975; the historic tower is preserved.
First-order rotating Fresnel, 1870 (Coast Pilot 1889; USCG table).

Point Reyes forms the seaward hazard of the Gulf of the Farallones on the approach to San Francisco, and is by official record the windiest and foggiest station on the Pacific coast (USCG pamphlet, 1962); a first-order headland light of the post-war program (MPS).
1975, when the Coast Guard installed automated equipment and retired the historic light (USCG table: automated/deactivated 1975).
Historic lens light retired 1975; the station remains an active aid via the adjacent automated beacon (Light List 2025, Fl W 5s, horn).
Transferred to the National Park Service; exhibit within Point Reyes National Seashore (USCG; NPS inventory).
Listed 1991-09-03, ref 91001100, Light Stations of California MPS (NRIS).

The Coast Guard's own 1962 description: "Point Reyes is, by official records, the windiest and foggiest on the Pacific Coast... few years pass that do not see violent gales of 75 to 100 mph strike the area," with keepers descending 304 steps to the lantern (quoted on the USCG page).

features.name: Farallon Islands Light (Southeast Farallon)

date.display: 1855 per USCG Historian's Office and NPS inventory ('Station Established: 1855 / First Lit

features.summary: The Farallones light, raised in 1855 on the granite peak of Southeast Farallon, was among the first cohort of Pacific lights and among the hardest built, with every brick packed uphill by hand. Its first-order lens covered the fog-bound outer approach to San Francisco for over a century; the tower, automated in 1972 and stripped of its lantern, still flashes over a national wildlife refuge.
facts: 1855 per USCG Historian's Office and NPS inventory ("Station Established: 1855 / First Lit: 1855"); the tower was well advanced in October 1855 (Bache to the Board, Annual Report 1855, appendix 25) and the first-order lens was first exhibited on 1 January 1856 in the standard accounts. The first tower of 1853-54 had to be rebuilt before the lens fit.

Brick-lined stone conical tower on the 360-ft summit of Southeast Farallon, built 1855 with brick carried up the rock 'in bundles of four and five on the backs of men' (USCG); lantern room later removed and replaced by an automatic beacon on the tower (USCG photo captions show the tower with and without lantern).
Guarded the deadly outer approach to Gold Rush San Francisco; the USCG narrative cites clippers such as the Golden City, detained five days off the Farallones in fog in 1852, as evidence of the need.
Never; active (Light List 2025, Fl W 15s, white conical tower).
Active aid within the Farallon National Wildlife Refuge (NPS inventory); island research station.
The islands were listed as the 'Farallone Islands' district, ref 77000332, on 1977-03-08 (NRIS); the lighthouse is within that listing.

For years a station mule - at one point 'the oldest inhabitant' - carried supplies up the rock; commercial egg-gathering for the San Francisco market and sealing went on around the keepers until the federal government stopped both (USCG page).

date.display: Fog-signal station established February 1875 (USCG pamphlet); 'Point Montara served exclus

features.summary: Montara began in February 1875 as a fog-signal station answering the wrecks on the ledges south of San Francisco, and only grew a light by stages: a small beacon around 1900, a fourth-order lens on a wooden tower in 1912, and the present little cast-iron tower in 1928. In 1912 a 4th order Fresnel lens was put atop a wooden tower" (NRHP nomination 91001094; the same document elsewhere says a beacon was added in 1902 - internal conflict noted). Present tower erected 1928.

date.display: Fog whistle 1872

features.summary: Año Nuevo was a fog station first and a lighthouse second: the government set a steam whistle on the islet in 1872 and added a five-story tower only in 1890. A buoy replaced the whole apparatus in 1948, and the island's keeper buildings have been decaying amid elephant seals and cormorants inside a state park ever since.
facts: Fog whistle 1872; light tower 1890: "In 1872, the federal government installed a fog whistle on the island and added a five-story light tower in 1890" (California State Parks, Año Nuevo SP brochure). The 1889 Coast Pilot confirms a steam fog-whistle, and no light, on the islet in 1889.

1872 steam fog-signal station on the islet off Point Año Nuevo; keeper's house (1872-era, now a seabird roost per State Parks); five-story light tower added 1890; station replaced by an automatic buoy in 1948 and left in arrested decay (State Parks brochure).
Not verified in located sources (USCG's state page carries an empty data block for this station; photo captions distinguish the 1872 and 1890 structures).

Station discontinued rather than automated: "An automatic buoy replaced the light tower in 1948, eliminating the need for lighthouse staff" (State Parks).
1948 (State Parks brochure). Today the Light List shows only Ano Nuevo Island Lighted Whistle Buoy 24 (LLNR 315).
Abandoned in place since 1948 within Año Nuevo State Park; buildings surrendered to seabirds and pinnipeds ('a state of arrested decay,' State Parks).

features.name: Santa Cruz Light Station

date.display: Original wooden lighthouse dates from 1869 (USCG: established/first lit 1869); the Coast P

features.summary: Santa Cruz's little wooden harbor light of 1869-70 spent seven decades marking the wharves of Monterey Bay's north shore under just three keepers, most famously Laura Hecox. Discontinued in 1941 and razed in 1948, it was succeeded in spirit and function by the Mark Abbott Memorial Lighthouse, a 1960s brick memorial that now carries the official Santa Cruz Light and a surfing museum.
facts: Original wooden lighthouse dates from 1869 (USCG: established/first lit 1869); the Coast Pilot 1889 records the fifth-order light 'first exhibited [month illegible] 1, 1870' - the two sources likely reflect completion (1869) versus first exhibition (1870).

1869 wooden dwelling with square tower at Point Santa Cruz; moved 300 ft inland 1878 due to erosion; light discontinued 1941; structure sold 1948 and razed in May 1948 (USCG). Brick Mark Abbott Memorial Lighthouse built near the site by the Abbott family after their son drowned surfing in 1965, using the lantern room from the Oakland Harbor Light; it carries today's Santa Cruz Light (USCG; Light List).
Fifth-order Fresnel, fixed red (Coast Pilot 1889); a fourth-order lens installed 1909 (USCG).

Served the narrow-gauge port and coastal trade of Santa Cruz on Monterey Bay (MPS context lists Santa Cruz among the narrow-gauge outlets; Coast Pilot's sailing directions key on the light for the wharves).
No - the original station was keeper-run to the end (last keeper Arthur Anderson until 1941, USCG).
1941 (USCG); the present Santa Cruz Light (Fl W 5s) is the memorial tower, home of the Santa Cruz Surfing Museum.
Original razed May 1948; successor brick tower stands as museum and active aid.

Laura Hecox succeeded her father A.A. Hecox as keeper in 1883 and served until her retirement in 1916 or 1917 (the Coast Guard's station page and its women-keepers list disagree) — a tenure of 33 or 34 years; only three keepers ran the light in its whole life (USCG). Her natural-history collection seeded the Santa Cruz city museum (tertiary; not verified).

features.name: Point Pinos Light Station

date.display: 1855 (USCG: established/first lit 1855

features.summary: Point Pinos, lit in 1855, is the oldest continuously operating lighthouse on the Pacific coast of the United States, still showing its original French third-order lens from the original granite Cape Cod building. Its early keepers included two notable women, Charlotte Layton and Emily Fish. Automated in 1975, it now belongs to the City of Pacific Grove.
facts: 1855 (USCG: established/first lit 1855; NRHP nomination 77000312: 'completed in 1855, shortly after Alcatraz Light'). The customary day, 1 February 1855, is tertiary-level in this survey. Oldest continuously operating lighthouse on the West Coast (USCG).

1855 granite Cape Cod dwelling with central conical brick tower - the original structure still in service; the third-order lens likewise original and operational (USCG; Coast Pilot 1889 describes the gray granite dwelling and round white tower).
Third-order Fresnel, purchased in France, in continuous use ("Even the original lens is still operational," USCG; nomination concurs).
Marked the southern entrance of Monterey Bay for the port of Monterey, one of the first cohort of eight Pacific lighthouses of the 1850s (MPS context; Coast Pilot).
Standing; light transferred to the City of Pacific Grove in 2006; museum (USCG).

First keeper Charles Layton died in office; local citizens petitioned the Lighthouse Board to appoint his widow Charlotte Layton keeper, and another woman, Emily Fish, later held the post; Robert Louis Stevenson visited and wrote about the light (USCG page).

features.name: Point Sur Light Station

date.display: 1889 (USCG: "The lighthouse was completed in 1889"; NRHP nomination 91001097 dates the tow

features.summary: Raised in 1889 from sandstone quarried on its own rock, Point Sur put a first-order light on the wild Big Sur coast after a decade of petitioning. Its complete hilltop station - tower, fog signal and dwellings - survived isolation, automation in 1972, and transfer to California State Parks, making it one of the most intact light stations in the state.

The customary day, 1 August 1889, is tertiary-level here.

1889 sandstone tower and fog-signal building quarried on site, on the great rock ('Morro Rock') of Point Sur, with keepers' dwellings of 1889/1902 above; funded 1886 after 11 years of petitions (USCG).

'Point Sur has always been a navigational nightmare' (USCG); the isolated Big Sur coast between Pigeon Point/Pinos and Piedras Blancas lacked any light, and the Coast Pilot of 1889 stresses the need on this bold stretch.
Standing; transferred to California State Parks (Point Sur State Historic Park; USCG).
Listed 1991-09-03, ref 91001097, Light Stations of California MPS (NRIS).
Keepers received goods by lighthouse tender roughly every four months, the Monterey trail being 'long and treacherous' (USCG).

features.name: Piedras Blancas Light Station

date.display: 1875 (NRHP nomination 91001095: "The lighthouse itself dates from 1875," significant dates

features.summary: Piedras Blancas raised a tall first-order brick tower on the white guano rocks north of San Simeon in 1875, closing one of the longest unlit reaches of the coast. Earthquake damage cost it its lantern room, giving the tower its distinctive flat top, but its light never stopped; it was automated in 1975 and now anchors a protected coastal research station.
facts: 1875 (NRHP nomination 91001095: "The lighthouse itself dates from 1875," significant dates 1875/1906; USCG: station established 1872, tower first lit 1875). The customary day, 15 February 1875, is tertiary-level here; the NPS inventory's '(1879)' is an outlier against both the nomination and USCG and is treated as an error.

1875 brick conical tower of the tall 'Middle Atlantic' type (MPS); lantern and upper tower removed after mid-20th-century earthquake damage, leaving the flat-topped tower in today's Light List description ("White conical tower with a flat top").
First-order Fresnel by Henry-Lepaute, 1875 (USCG table: "FIRST ORDER (made by Henri Lapaute) 1875"). The lens's later display in Cambria is a tertiary lead, not verified here.

Covered the 94-mile dark gap of the south-central coast and the whaling and coastal anchorage at San Simeon (nomination context; the San Luis Obispo nomination measures the Arguello-Piedras Blancas gap).

Standing (truncated); active aid and research station (NPS inventory 2003); managed since 2001 as BLM's Piedras Blancas Light Station Outstanding Natural Area (tertiary; not verified in located records).

features.name: San Luis Obispo Light Station (Port Harford)

date.display: Completed 30 June 1890: 'the station was not completed until June 30, 1890' (NRHP nominati

features.summary: The Port Harford light of 30 June 1890 answered the Queen of the Pacific's 1888 sinking and the long dark gap of the south-central coast, planting a gingerbread Stick-style dwelling-tower on Point San Luis. It is the only one of its three identical 1890 sisters still standing, its fourth-order lens now in county museum hands and its buildings restored for visitors.

Fourth-order Fresnel (USCG); replaced by a modern beacon in 1969, lens moved 1976 to the San Luis Obispo County Historical Society (USCG).

Port Harford (Avila) was the coastal outlet of San Luis Obispo and 'one of the most active ports between San Francisco and San Diego,' with no light in the 94 miles between Point Arguello and Piedras Blancas; the sinking of the steamer Queen of the Pacific on 30 April 1888 clinched the appropriation (nomination).
1975 as a staffed lighthouse; the site still shows a light (Light List 2025, Fl W 5s, lighted 24 hours).

features.name: Point Arguello Light Station

date.display: 1901: "In 1901, the lighthouse service built a light station at Point Arguello" (USCG Hist

features.summary: Point Arguello, where the Yankee Blade went down in 1854 and seven Navy destroyers piled up at Honda Point in 1923, got its light station only in 1901. The original lighthouse gave way in the 1930s to a rotating aerobeacon, and today a simple post light on the Vandenberg coast carries on the station's warning at the west door of the Santa Barbara Channel.
facts: 1901: "In 1901, the lighthouse service built a light station at Point Arguello" (USCG Historian's Office). The Board's own list of new lights for 1901 (p. 11) records a fourth-order light established 22 February 1901.

1901 lighthouse (original tower later removed); by 1968 the station showed a 36-inch rotating aerobeacon of 1,100,000 cp on a structure 124 ft above the water, with two-tone diaphone and radiobeacon (USCG 1968 description; photo captions distinguish 'the original Point Arguello light tower' and 'the Point Arguello skeleton tower'). Today a post light (Light List).
Original apparatus not verified in located sources (commonly given as a fourth-order Fresnel - tertiary only).

The 'Graveyard of the Pacific' at the west entrance of the Santa Barbara Channel: the Yankee Blade wrecked there 1 October 1854 with about 415 lives and a bullion cargo, and shipwrecks continued for half a century before the 1901 station (USCG narrative). The same rocks later claimed seven destroyers and 22 men in the Honda Point disaster of 8 September 1923 (USCG narrative gives September 9).
1966-era remote operation implied; explicit automation year not verified (USCG page's structured block is empty for Arguello).
Never as a station site; the aid persists as a post light (Light List 2025, Fl W 15s). The 1901 tower itself is gone (replacement commonly dated 1934 - tertiary).
Original structures removed; site within Vandenberg Space Force Base; modern minor aid remains.
The station doubled as a key synoptic weather reporting point for national weather maps, and its associated Coast Guard lifeboat station (est. 1934-38) served until 1958 (USCG).

features.name: Point Conception Light Station

date.display: First lighted 1 February 1856 (NRHP nomination 81000176 narrative: the PIERCE delivered le

features.summary: One of the original eight Pacific lighthouses, Point Conception first showed its French first-order light on 1 February 1856 at the hinge of the California coast. The station moved partway down its bluff in 1881-82 to escape the high fog, and the 1882 tower still turns the 1856 lens - among the longest-serving optics in the country. It was automated in 1973 and remains active.
facts: First lighted 1 February 1856 (NRHP nomination 81000176 narrative: the PIERCE delivered lens and lamp and the light was exhibited 'February 1, 1856'); lower replacement tower first lit 1882 (USCG: established 1856, current tower 1881-82).

1856 tower and dwelling high on the bluff (razed; the nomination notes the original 1854-era lighthouse site presumably destroyed with 1960s razing of buildings); station relocated 1881 to a mesa 133 ft above the sea and the present tower lit 1882 after the Fort Tejon earthquake of 9 January 1857 had earlier damaged the first building (USCG narrative, which misdates the quake to 1867).
First-order Fresnel, 1856, still in use at the time of listing ('still utilizes its original lens,' nomination; USCG concurs "FIRST ORDER, FRESNEL 1856").

The 'Cape Horn of the Pacific' - the great turning point between the coastwise route and the Santa Barbara Channel, part of the first 1850s cohort; the lens and ironwork came around Cape Horn from France at a cost of $65,068 (USCG).
Standing; active USCG aid on private ranch coast (access restricted).

features.summary: Santa Barbara's 1856 lighthouse was a classic first-generation dwelling-tower, best remembered for Julia Williams's forty-year vigil over its fixed light. features.name: Los Angeles Harbor Light Station (Angels Gate)

date.display: 1913 (USCG: established/first lit 1913

features.summary: 'Angels Gate' has stood at the end of the San Pedro breakwater since 1913, a Romanesque concrete cylinder that survived a five-day storm with nothing worse than a permanent lean. Its green flash and foghorns - Moaning Maggie, then Blatting Betty - defined the harbor entrance of Los Angeles; the keepers left on 1 February 1973 when the light was automated.

features.name: Old Point Loma Lighthouse

date.display: 15 November 1855: "Point Loma Lighthouse was put into service on November 15, 1855" (NPS C

features.summary: The 1855 Old Point Loma light crowned its headland so high that fog regularly blotted it out, an elegant failure of the first Pacific cohort. Extinguished on 23 March 1891 in favor of the new tower at the point's tip, it was saved by its inclusion in Cabrillo National Monument and a 1930s restoration, and is now among the most-visited lighthouses in the country.
facts: 15 November 1855: "Point Loma Lighthouse was put into service on November 15, 1855" (NPS Cabrillo NM webpage; USCG concurs: "First lighted November 15, 1855").

Structure completed 1854 (architect Ammi B. Young, Treasury Dept.; contractors Gibbons & Kelly, Baltimore); sandstone/brick Cape Cod dwelling with central tower at 422-462 ft elevation - at the time the highest light in the U.S.; restored by the NPS 1933-35 (USCG; NPS; nomination notes 3rd-order lens installed November 1855).
Third-order fixed Fresnel from Sautter & Co., Paris, $3,810 - the lens originally intended for Humboldt Harbor (USCG page).
First lighthouse of Southern California, in the initial 1850s Pacific cohort, marking San Diego Bay; sited too high, 'too often, its light was obscured by fog and low clouds' (NPS Cabrillo).
23 March 1891, when the lens was removed and the new lower station took over (USCG; NPS: "A new Point Loma Light Station was established at a lower elevation in March 1891").
Preserved centerpiece of Cabrillo National Monument (proclaimed 1913); restored 1933-35; displays a third-order lens (NPS; USCG).
Robert Israel kept the old light for 18 years and personally lit the new station's kerosene lamp on 23 March 1891, serving one more year there (NPS Cabrillo NM page).

features.summary: From 1898 the San Francisco lightship rode outside the bar where Alcatraz and Fort Point ranged in line, showing masthead electric lanterns to funnel traffic into the Golden Gate's main ship channel. Five vessels held the station over 73 years - LV-70, LV-83, WLV-612 and LV-100 among them - until a lighted horn buoy replaced the last ship in 1971.

'The station marked the approaches to the main ship channel into San Francisco' outside the bar (USCG Lightship Station Index).

In August 1899 LV-70 hosted a 17-day experiment in wireless telegraphy - among the earliest marine radio trials on the Pacific coast (USCG LV-70 page).

features.summary: The Blunts Reef lightship tossed off Cape Mendocino from 1905, holding coastwise traffic clear of the reef that the cape's high light could not adequately cover in fog. LV-83's rescue of 155 souls from the steamer Bear in 1916 made it famous; buoys replaced the ships in 1971, and one veteran of the station, WLV-605 RELIEF, survives on the National Register at Oakland.

features.name: Alcatraz Island Light

date.display: June 1, 1854

features.summary: Alcatraz carried what the standard accounts call the Pacific coast's first lighthouse: a Gibbons & Kelly contract dwelling finished in 1853 that finally showed its third-order light on June 1, 1854, once the lens arrived. After the 1906 earthquake cracked the old building and the new cell house crowded it, the Lighthouse Service transferred the light on December 1, 1909 to the present 84-foot octagonal concrete tower, a move documented in the printed Notice to Mariners of December 2, 1909. Automated in 1963 during the island's federal-prison era, the tower still operates inside Golden Gate NRA.
facts: exact day from lighthousefriends.com (citing Lighthouse Board annual reports; primary report not directly examined); 'first on the West Coast' corroborated by NPS (nps.gov/alca history page: 'first lighthouse on the West Coast') and by a primary federal source, Annual Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses FY1915, which exhibits 'the first lens used on the Pacific coast at Alcatraz, Cal., in 1854.' Fort Point's 1853 building was structurally finished earlier but was demolished unlit, and the next lights (Point Pinos Feb. 1855, Fort Point Mar. 1855) followed Alcatraz - lighthousefriends' Fort Point page calls Fort Point 'the third lighthouse to be activated on the west coast,' consistent with Alcatraz first.

June 1, 1854 — the first lighthouse lighted on the US Pacific coast. Fort Point's 1853 building was structurally finished earlier but was demolished unlit, and the next lights (Point Pinos Feb. 1855, Fort Point Mar. 1855) followed Alcatraz - lighthousefriends' Fort Point page calls Fort Point 'the third lighthouse to be activated on the west coast,' consistent with Alcatraz first.

1) 1852-54: Cape Cod-style dwelling with central tower, one of the Gibbons & Kelly contract lighthouses; completed by July 1853, lit June 1, 1854 (fixed 3rd-order lens). 2) 1909: 84-ft gray octagonal pyramidal reinforced-concrete tower with attached keepers' dwelling, built after 1906 earthquake damage and cell-house construction; light moved to the new tower December 1, 1909 (primary: Notice to Mariners, 12th District, Dec. 2, 1909, printed in San Francisco Call, Dec. 3, 1909, p. 15: 'on December 1, 1909, the light at this station was moved to and established in the new tower').

Original: fixed third-order Fresnel, 1854 (USCG Historian). 1902: revolving two-panel fourth-order Fresnel, white flash every 15s (lighthousefriends). Modern: rotating aerobeacon, Fl W 5s (Light List 2025).

features.name: Fort Point Light

date.display: March 1855 (second tower; commonly given as March 21, 1855 - day not independently verifie

features.summary: Fort Point ran through three lighthouses in eleven years: the 1853 contract tower was torn down unlit to make way for the brick fort, its 1855 wooden replacement was lit in March 1855 as the third light on the coast, and an iron nine-sided tower rose over the fort's stairwell in 1863-64 when the seawall forced another demolition. The Golden Gate Bridge finally made the station redundant, and the light was extinguished on September 1, 1934. The little iron tower survives on the fort, now a National Historic Site.
facts: lighthousefriends ("In March 1855, the light from a fifth-order Fresnel lens... was exhibited for the first time, making it the third lighthouse to be activated on the west coast"); USCG Historian gives 'Date built 1853' for the never-lit first tower.

March 1855 (second tower; commonly given as March 21, 1855 - day not independently verified). Grade: lighthousefriends ("In March 1855, the light from a fifth-order Fresnel lens... was exhibited for the first time, making it the third lighthouse to be activated on the west coast"); USCG Historian gives 'Date built 1853' for the never-lit first tower.

1) 1852-53 Gibbons & Kelly tower, complete 1853 but demolished before its lens arrived to clear the site for Fort Winfield Scott (its intended third-order lens went to Point Pinos - lighthousefriends). 2) 1855: 36-ft wooden tower between fort and seawall, lit March 1855; demolished 1863 for seawall work (USCG Historian). 3) 1863-64: 27-ft nine-sided iron-plate tower on the fort's northwest stair tower, focal plane ~83-110 ft; USCG Historian dates the present tower 1864, lighthousefriends 1863.
First tower: none installed. Second: fifth-order Fresnel (lighthousefriends). Third: fourth-order Fresnel (USCG Historian); lens changes 1878, 1903, 1912 (lighthousefriends).
To mark the south side of the Golden Gate itself for vessels running the narrows (USCG Historian; lighthousefriends).

September 1, 1934, because Golden Gate Bridge construction (and the bridge itself) obstructed and superseded the light (USCG Historian: 'Deactivated in 1934'; lighthousefriends: "On September 1, 1934, Fort Point Lighthouse ceased operation").

features.summary: Point Bonita's 1855 lighthouse was built too high: at 306 feet its second-order light sat above the fog it was meant to pierce, so in 1877 the Service tunneled through the headland and re-erected the lantern on the wave-cut outer point, where it was relit on February 1, 1877. features.name: Mile Rocks Light

date.display: February 15, 1906

features.summary: The loss of the City of Rio de Janeiro in the fog off Fort Point in February 1901 pushed Congress to fund a lighthouse on Mile Rocks, a pair of wave-washed rocks a mile off Lands End. Crews working from a schooner bolted a steel-cased caisson to the larger rock and stacked a three-tier steel tower above it, lighting it on February 15, 1906. In 1965-66 the Coast Guard decapitated the tower for a helipad and automated the light, which still flashes from the surviving base.

quotes.text: 28. Mile Rocks, southern side of channel, entrance to San Francisco Bay, California.—Contracts were made for building the concrete and steel substructure and also for the steel superstructure of the station. Work under the first contract was commenced in August, 1904, when a working party landed on the rock and commenced preparing it, by cutting and blasting, to receive the foundations of the building. In September, 1904, a schooner fitted as quarters for the workmen and for the storage of materials was moored close to the rock, but during a heavy blow she dragged her moorings and barely escaped being wrecked. ... The work was difficult and hazardous during its early stages, and proceeded slowly on account of the exposed position of Mile Rocks, directly in the entrance to San Francisco Harbor, where it is subjected to all the violence of the sea. There was hardly a day during the year on which at some time the waves did not break over the rock. There were many days when no landing could be effected and many others when the party, after landing, was driven off with only a few hours of work accomplished. On several occasions it was necessary to call upon the neighboring life-saving crews to take the men off the rock. A full day of eight hours passed upon the rock was exceptional until after the substructure was completed in June, 1905. This consists of a monolith of concrete inclosed within steel plates resting on the rock at the level of mean high water. It is elliptical in plan, covering 704 square feet, and has a height of 34 feet; 1,006 barrels of cement, furnished by the Government, were used in the work.

features.summary: Southampton Shoal received a cottage-style lighthouse on iron cylinders in December 1905, guarding the shoal on the run from the central bay toward San Pablo Bay. The 1906 earthquake racked its legs; braces and rock held it for another half-century of keepers until Point Blunt assumed its fog signal in 1960. In 1966 the wooden dwelling was barged to Tinsley Island in the delta as a yacht-club outstation, and an automated tower on the old site still marks the shoal.

Two-story square wooden dwelling with pyramidal roof, dormers, and cylindrical lantern on a platform carried by eleven iron/concrete foundation cylinders driven into the shoal ($30,000 appropriated March 3, 1903; contract March 1905). The April 1906 earthquake tilted the cylinders up to eleven degrees, requiring cross-bracing and rock fill (lighthousefriends, citing LHB reports).

The 1906 earthquake reached even this water station, tilting its legs eastward - reported through the Lighthouse Board's engineering correspondence (as summarized by lighthousefriends).

features.name: East Brother Island Light Station

date.display: March 1, 1874; fog signal in operation May 1, 1874

features.summary: Built in 1873-74 on a dynamited islet off Point San Pablo, East Brother lighted the strait between San Francisco and San Pablo Bays from March 1, 1874, its steam whistle following that May. The Victorian tower-dwelling, cistern, and fog-signal building survived earthquake, automation in 1969, and a demolition plan, becoming one of the first West Coast light stations rescued by NRHP listing. A nonprofit has operated it as an inn since 1980, with the light still flashing.
facts: PRIMARY-adjacent - the NRHP nomination text (1971), drawing on the station file and LHB Annual Reports 1873-74: "The light was exhibited for the first time on March 1st, and the fog signal was put in operation on May 1st of that year."

March 1, 1874; fog signal in operation May 1, 1874. Grade: PRIMARY-adjacent - the NRHP nomination text (1971), drawing on the station file and LHB Annual Reports 1873-74: "The light was exhibited for the first time on March 1st, and the fog signal was put in operation on May 1st of that year."

Two-story Victorian ('Carpenter Gothic'/Stick style) combined tower-and-dwelling, fog-signal building, shop/storage building, wharf, water tank, and a blasted 30-ft-deep cistern, all on a leveled one-acre rock; built 1873-74 after Maj. George H. Elliott, Engineer Secretary of the Light-House Board, obtained the War Department's release of the easterly Brother island in February 1873 and Congress appropriated $30,000 (NRHP nomination). Design attributed to Lighthouse Board draftsman Paul J. Pelz (Wikipedia/Perry attribution; the nomination says only 'an East Coast lighthouse designer').
Fourth-order Fresnel; the original lens was cracked in the 1906 earthquake and replaced by a new Paris-made lens used until automation (NRHP nomination; USCG Historian: fourth order).

Mainland-site litigation being impracticable, the Board took the island to light San Pablo Strait - the narrow passage every vessel bound to Mare Island Navy Yard, Carquinez, and the river ports must thread (NRHP nomination). This IS the 'San Pablo Straits' station: no separate San Pablo Strait lighthouse ever existed.
1969 (NRHP nomination-era text; USCG Historian: "Automated: 1969, now FA 251").
Never - active aid, Fl W 5s (Light List 2025).

Slated for demolition after automation, the station was saved by its 1971 NRHP listing and since 1980 has been run as a bed-and-breakfast inn by the nonprofit East Brother Light Station, Inc. (founded 1979) under USCG license; the light and (winter) fog horn remain active (Wikipedia; Light List 2025).

Keeper John Stenmark (1894-1914), a Swedish-born sailor rewarded with the post for rescues, raised four children on the one-acre rock; two were born on the island after he rowed to Point San Quentin for the doctor (NRHP nomination). features.name: Mare Island Light

date.display: September 1, 1873 (lighthouse completed July 15, 1873)

features.summary: Lighted on September 1, 1873 at the southeastern tip of the Navy Yard island, Mare Island Light was East Brother's near-twin, a Victorian tower-dwelling with a fourth-order fixed white light and a fog bell moved up from Point Bonita. It is remembered for Kate McDougal, appointed in December 1881 months after her husband, the district's lighthouse inspector, drowned at Cape Mendocino, and keeper here for some 35 years until the light's discontinuation on July 1, 1917, by which time the new Carquinez Strait Light half a mile off had taken its work. The Navy razed the empty buildings in the 1930s; only the site remains, on the former shipyard.
facts: tertiary quoting primary - lighthousefriends quotes the LHB Annual Report 1873 ("The light-house of this station was completed by the 15th of July, although it was not quite ready for lighting at that date") and gives the September 1, 1873 in-operation date; USCG Historian: 'Date Built: 1873.' September 1, 1873 (lighthouse completed July 15, 1873). Combined square tower and two-story wood dwelling (a near-sister of East Brother's Victorian design - USCG Historian: 'very similar to San Francisco's East Brother Lighthouse'; Wikipedia attributes the design to Paul J. Pelz), with fog bell (a bell relocated from Cape Mendocino; moved to the wharf end 1893), 15,000-gal water tank (1877), landing wharf (1892); bell striker automated 1916 (USCG Historian; lighthousefriends).
Fourth-order Fresnel, fixed white (USCG Historian; lighthousefriends).

To light the deep-water approach past the Navy Yard: every vessel entering Mare Island Strait for the yard, or Carquinez Strait for Benicia, Port Costa, and the river trade, rounded this point. Its replacement logic ran the same way - the taller 1910 Carquinez Strait Light 9/16 mile away made it redundant (1910 notice; USCG Historian).
Fog bell machinery automated 1916; the light itself was discontinued rather than automated (USCG Historian).
July 1, 1917 (lighthousefriends; USCG Historian: 'Deactivated in 1917'). Superseded by Carquinez Strait Light (est. Jan. 15, 1910).

Buildings stood into the interwar Navy era and were razed in the 1930s (USCG Historian; lighthousefriends). The site lies on the former Mare Island Naval Shipyard; Wikipedia notes a Navy direction-finding station occupied it 1942-45, then a Navy radiobeacon. Nothing of the lighthouse survives above ground.
No individual listing; the site is within the Mare Island NHL district boundary context (shipyard NHL) - contributing status NOT verified this session.

Kate Caffrey McDougal kept this light for 35+ years (appointed December 1881; USCG Historian's women-keepers list: "Appointed keeper in December 1881; 1881-1916"; lighthousefriends, from service records and census: served until her resignation May 22, 1917, weeks before the light was discontinued; died 1932, age 90). Her husband, Cmdr. Charles J. McDougal USN, 12th District lighthouse inspector, drowned on the morning of March 28, 1881 when his boat capsized landing at Cape Mendocino Light from the tender Manzanita - PRIMARY: Sacramento Daily Record-Union, March 29, 1881, p.1 ("Captain McDougall, Lighthouse Inspector, with two others, was drowned off Mendocino light while attempting to go ashore from the steamer Ma[n]zanita... this morning"). The Lighthouse Board then gave the widow the bay's gentlest station, a few miles from the Navy Yard where the couple had been posted. Daughter Elizabeth M. McDougal (b. Washington DC 1870, 'daughter of Charles J. and Kate Caffrey McDougal') later worked in the 5th District office 1893-98 (USCG women-keepers list). CAUTION: the USLHS 'In Memoriam' roster instead records "Charles J. McDougal, District Inspector, Punta Gorda CA, March 5, 1909, Drowned" - irreconcilable with the 1881 contemporary press; either a roster error or a same-named son. Flagged, unresolved. Also note the first keeper, 1873-1881, was a woman, Theresa C. Watson (lighthousefriends keeper list) - meaning every head keeper from 1873 to May 1917 was a woman; a man, Angus Murray, tended the light only through its last weeks before discontinuance.

No published position in allowed sources located (station razed; not in modern Light List/GNIS as a light). Site: the southeastern tip of Mare Island commanding the entrances to Carquinez and Mare Island Straits - USCG Historian: "North shore of San Pablo Bay at the entrance to Carquinez Strait"; the 1910 Carquinez notice places Carquinez Strait Light ~9/16 mile at 106°30' true FROM Mare Island lighthouse. GNIS island record 228080 (Mare Island). lighthousefriends map point 38.0769, -122.2527 is tertiary, lead only.

features.name: Carquinez Strait Light

date.display: January 15, 1910

features.summary: Established January 15, 1910 on piles at the mouth of Mare Island Strait, the Carquinez Strait Light packed tower, fog signal, and a 28-room dwelling into one enormous wooden building at the end of a long dike - the inland gatepost for river-bound shipping, replacing the little Mare Island light half a mile away. The Coast Guard abandoned the building for automatic aids in 1951, and in 1955 the whole structure was barged to Glen Cove, where it still stands, de-towered, as a marina office. The station function itself was automated in 1963.
facts: PRIMARY - period Notice to Mariners, 12th District, printed in the San Francisco Call, Jan. 19, 1910, p.15: "Carquinez strait light station was established January 15, 1910, in the structure recently erected..."; light fixed red, fourth order, 56 ft above water, visible 13 miles, cream-colored square tower rising from a 2.5-story dwelling and fog-signal building on piles in 8 ft of water.

Grade: PRIMARY - period Notice to Mariners, 12th District, printed in the San Francisco Call, Jan. 19, 1910, p.15: "Carquinez strait light station was established January 15, 1910, in the structure recently erected..."; light fixed red, fourth order, 56 ft above water, visible 13 miles, cream-colored square tower rising from a 2.5-story dwelling and fog-signal building on piles in 8 ft of water.

A single huge combined structure: 28-room 2.5-story dwelling with attached three-story tower and fog-signal wing, on piles at the end of a long pier/dike (~150 tons; $50,000 appropriated March 4, 1907; built Aug. 1908-late 1909) (1910 notice; USCG 1966 press release text on the Historian's page; lighthousefriends).

Fourth-order Fresnel, fixed red (1910 notice: 'fixed red, of the [fourth] order'; USCG Historian: Fourth Order Fresnel). The station also served as a test platform for vertical 'mushroom' trumpet fog signals (USCG Historian).

The Lighthouse Board pressed Congress for a major light between San Francisco Bay and the Sacramento River to serve traffic into Carquinez and Mare Island Straits; it superseded the 1873 Mare Island light across the channel (USCG Historian; 1910 notice geometry).
June 3, 1963 - light and fog signal automated when USCG personnel left the replacement bluff-top station (USCG 1966 press release on Historian's page).

Lighthouse building abandoned as an aid in 1951, when an automatic beacon and fog signal were set on the pier and new family quarters were built on the bluff above (USCG press release; the Historian's summary card says 'Deactivated 1951').

On August 6, 1955 the 150-ton building was jacked onto a barge and towed two miles to Elliott Cove (Glen Cove), Vallejo; tower removed; the dwelling survives as the Glen Cove Marina office and event space (USCG 1966 press release: 'taken off its pilings and put aboard a barge... towed two miles to its new location at Elliott Cove'; lighthousefriends adds the 1955 purchase by contractor Robert Hubert and current marina use).

Original station site: published 1910 description only - 'on the northerly side of the entrance to Carquinez strait and the easterly side of the entrance to Napa creek, just inside of the long wooden dike, about 9/16 mile 106°30' true from Mare Island lighthouse' (Notice to Mariners, Jan. 1910); modern minor aids mark the vicinity (Light List 2025 Carquinez Strait lights). Relocated building at Glen Cove Marina, Vallejo (lighthousefriends map point 38.0678, -122.2137 - tertiary lead).

quotes.text: Carquinez Strait light-station, California.—The act approved March 4, 1907, appropriated $50,000 for the establishment of a light and fog-signal station at Carquinez Strait, between San Pablo Bay and Suisun Bay, authorized by the act approved February 26, 1907. The actual work of construction was commenced August 4, 1908. The station was established January 15, 1910. A fourth-order fixed red light and two gasoline-engine compressed-air plants operating 6-inch first-class compressed-air sirens were installed. The superstructure consists of a frame tower for the light, a frame dwelling with quarters for three keepers, a frame fog-signal house, a frame boathouse, a galvanized-iron oil house, and distillate house. A water pipe connects with the Vallejo city mains. Total cost of constructing station, $48,296.17.
quotes.cite: Report of the Light-House Board, printed in the Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, FY1910 (Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1910; 'Report of the Operations of the Light-House Board'), p. 508

quotes.text: Carquinez Strait, California.—Authorized by the act of February 26, 1907, at a cost not to exceed $50,000; appropriation, act of March 4, 1907, $50,000. During the year the contractor commenced work on the landing and approach, the station substructure on piles, and on the superstructure, the latter consisting of a light and fog-signal building, boathouse, and three sets of keepers' quarters. At the close of the year he had practically completed the station substructure and the landing and approach. The superstructure is about 65 per cent completed. As soon as the contract is completed, which will probably be in July of the coming year, the fourth-order lens, lantern, fog-signal machinery, and 6-inch standard sirens, which are all on hand, will be installed, and the station should be ready for operation about October 1, 1909.

features.name: Roe Island Light

date.display: February 16, 1891, first keeper Richard A. Weiss (lighthousefriends: Weiss 'placed the sta

features.summary: The only staffed light station east of Carquinez Strait, Roe Island Light went into service on February 16, 1891, a low cottage lantern on pilings marking the Suisun Bay channel to the upriver ports. It survived half a century of fog and grain traffic only to be wrecked from within the bay: the Port Chicago explosion of July 17, 1944 tore its bell house loose from 3,000 yards away. Discontinued in 1945 and sold, the buildings later burned; only channel range lights carry the name today.
facts: tertiary quoting primary; USCG concurs on year.

February 16, 1891, first keeper Richard A. Weiss (lighthousefriends: Weiss 'placed the station in operation on February 16, 1891'; USCG Historian: established/first lit 1891). Grade: tertiary quoting primary; USCG concurs on year.

Square 1.5-story wooden dwelling on low pilings with veranda, dormers, and an octagonal roof lantern (light 41 ft above water, flashing white; fog bell, 1 stroke/10s, in a bell house on the T-pier), plus oil house, outbuildings, and a second dwelling added in the 1900s; land deeded by Dr. Washington M. Ryer; ironwork by M. A. Graham, buildings/wharf by California Bridge Co. (USCG Historian; lighthousefriends).

Fifth-order Fresnel, fixed white, 1891 — the Board's report for that year (p. 158) records a fixed white light exhibited when the station went into operation; the later flashing characteristic in the Coast Guard's records reflects a subsequent change, not the original apparatus.

To mark the Suisun Bay channel where deep-water traffic bound for Benicia, Port Costa wheat wharves, and the rivers threaded the shoals - 33 miles inside the Golden Gate, five miles east of Benicia, opposite what became Port Chicago (USCG Historian).

1945, after the Port Chicago explosion of July 17, 1944 (two ammunition ships, E. A. Bryan and Quinault Victory, detonated ~3,000 yards away, killing over 300, knocking the station's bell house off its foundation and smashing windows - USCG Historian, quoting an 11 Aug. 1944 USCG report on the station's composition; keeper Erven A. Scott's damage account in lighthousefriends). Channel changes had already reduced its value (USCG Historian).

Sold: the city of Pittsburg bought it in November 1946 for $4,000; Boy Scout use to 1953; later privately held as a summer place until fire destroyed the buildings (lighthousefriends; USCG Historian: 'sold... used as a summer home until a fire completely destroyed it'). Fire date not established. Roe Island Channel range lights remain in the 2025 Light List.

Keeper John M. Nilsson served ~21 years (1893-1914); last keeper Erven A. Scott rode out the Port Chicago blast in the station and reported furniture thrown about and every window gone (lighthousefriends).

quotes.text: 814. Roe Island, Suisun Bay, California.—Contracts for the construction of this station were let to Mr. M. A. Graham for the ironwork, and to the California Bridge Company for the construction of the buildings and wharf. Both contractors completed their work in a satisfactory manner and within the specified time. A small building, to contain the fog-bell machinery, was built on the outer end of the wharf, and a bell was purchased and hung. On February 16, 1891, the station was put in operation, when a fixed white light was exhibited from the lantern placed on top of the dwelling. It is of the fifth order, illuminating the entire horizon. The fog signal is a bell, which is struck by machinery one blow every ten seconds. During May a small oil house, a platform for coal, etc., under the wharf, and steps leading to the ground, were built.

quotes.text: 852. Roe Island, Suisun Bay, California.—A windmill and pump were placed on the outer end of the wharf and connection was made by pipe with the cistern to bring in a supply of fresh water. The lantern parapet was incased in redwood to prevent leakage. This island being subject to overflow at times of high water, a levee 3½ feet high by 8 feet at the base was built around the reservation. This levee was cracked in April by a severe earthquake, and it was repaired by the keeper.

features.name: Angel Island Light Station (Point Knox)

date.display: Fog bell in operation November 1, 1886 (appropriation $4,500, March 3, 1885

features.summary: Angel Island's light station began as a fog-bell post at Point Knox in November 1886, a bell house and cottage bolted to the island's fog-blind western bluff, gaining a small fixed-red light in 1900. Keeper Juliet Fish Nichols made it famous in July 1906 when the striking machinery shattered in dense fog and she beat the bell by hand through the night and the next day. After 1915 its keepers also ran the island's Point Stuart and Point Blunt minor lights; the station closed October 31, 1960 and was burned in 1963, leaving the bell standing in the state park.
facts: tertiary (lighthousefriends) quoting LHB annual reports and George Worthylake, 'Point Knox,' The Keeper's Log (Fall 1996); no primary directly examined this session.

Fog bell in operation November 1, 1886 (appropriation $4,500, March 3, 1885; work begun September 1885); a lens-lantern showing fixed red was added in November 1900. Grade: tertiary (lighthousefriends) quoting LHB annual reports and George Worthylake, 'Point Knox,' The Keeper's Log (Fall 1996); no primary directly examined this session.

Bell house and keeper's dwelling on a timber platform at the base of the bluff at Point Knox, reached by a long stairway; 3,000-lb bell struck by clockwork machinery; small lens-lantern light added 1900. From 1915 the station's keepers also tended the new Point Stuart and Point Blunt minor lights/sirens 1-2 miles away (lighthousefriends; USCG press release on Point Blunt entry: "Point Blunt Light was originally maintained by personnel at Angel Island Light Station at Point Knox").
Lens-lantern, fixed red, hung near the bell nightly from November 1900 (lighthousefriends).
To warn traffic in the fog-swept western angle of Angel Island, where the ebb sets vessels out of Raccoon Strait onto Point Knox shoal (Coast Pilot 1943 notes the shoal; lighthousefriends).
Station disestablished October 31, 1960, when the Coast Guard consolidated Angel Island operations at the new Point Blunt station (lighthousefriends; USCG press release: personnel moved 1960-61).
October 31, 1960 (as a staffed station); the Point Knox aid was replaced by a lighted gong buoy off the shoal (1988 Light List).

Abandoned structures deliberately burned in 1963; the great fog bell still stands in its frame on the point, within Angel Island State Park (lighthousefriends; the Southampton Shoal lens is displayed at the park's interpretive center - USCG Historian).
No individual listing found (the island's NHL listing is the US Immigration Station).

Juliet Fish Nichols, keeper 1902-1914 (USCG Historian's women-keepers list: "Juliet Nichols, Angel Island, CA, 1902-1914"), Shanghai-born (1859) widow of Cmdr. Henry Nichols USN (d. 1899 in the Philippines). Her station log for the July 1906 fog, as quoted in Worthylake's Keeper's Log article via lighthousefriends: "July 4 - ...8:00 p.m. machinery went to pieces - great tension bar broke in two - dense fog... bell struck with a nail hammer, standing out on the platform until 4 p.m. [July 5]." She hand-struck the 3,000-lb bell roughly 20 hours 35 minutes and received a special commendation (lighthousefriends/Worthylake).

GNIS gaz_id 254857 (Point Knox, Marin Co.); the station platform clung to the bluff at/below the point. 1988 Light List: Point Knox Lighted Gong Buoy 2 at 37°50.2'N 122°26.7'W marks the shoal offshore.

features.name: Point Stuart Light

date.display: Fiscal year 1915 (July 1914-June 1915)

features.summary: Point Stuart got its light and electric fog siren in fiscal 1915 as one of a pair of unwatched aids added to Angel Island and run by wire from the Point Knox keepers. A white frame signal house on the island's western nose, it marked the mouth of Raccoon Strait for seventy-odd years, latterly under the name Raccoon Strait Light, before being supplanted by a buoy. Its establishment is documented directly in the Commissioner of Lighthouses' FY1915 annual report.
facts: PRIMARY - Annual Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses FY1915, p.8: "Fog signals established: ... Point Blunt and Point Stuart, Angel Island, San Francisco Bay, Cal. (electric sirens)", with both points also in the report's new-minor-lights tabulation; lighthousefriends (from the same reports) describes remote-controlled 500-watt lamps in lens lanterns.

(electric sirens)", with both points also in the report's new-minor-lights tabulation; lighthousefriends (from the same reports) describes remote-controlled 500-watt lamps in lens lanterns.

Unwatched minor light and electric siren in a small white frame house on the island's westerly point (Coast Pilot 1943: "Point Stuart Light, shown from a white frame house, is 80 feet above water"; fog signal an air diaphragm horn by then), operated remotely by the Point Knox keepers a mile away (lighthousefriends; USCG press release).
Lens lantern with electric incandescent lamp (lighthousefriends, from Lighthouse Service records).
To light the southern entrance of Raccoon Strait and the island's western turning point for northbound bay traffic (Coast Pilot 1943 context; part of the 1915 Angel Island minor-aids scheme).
Remote/automatic from establishment; tended from Point Knox to 1960, then Point Blunt ("Raccoon Strait light and fog signals" operated by Point Blunt personnel - USCG July 1970 press release).

The shore light survived (as 'Raccoon Strait Light') at least into the late 1980s (1988 Light List); by the 2025 Light List only Raccoon Strait Lighted Buoy 1 remains - formal discontinuation date not established.
Frame structure gone; site within Angel Island State Park. No NRHP listing.

features.name: Point Blunt Light

date.display: Minor light and electric fog siren established fiscal year 1915 (PRIMARY: Commissioner of

features.summary: Point Blunt began in fiscal 1915 as the third of Angel Island's remotely run minor lights, but after WWII the Coast Guard reversed the automation tide here, building a full manned station between about 1957 and 1961 - the last lighthouse station built and staffed in California - whose watch room controlled its own light, Raccoon Strait's, and Southampton Shoal's. It was automated on June 28, 1976 and still shows a green flash over the anchorage approaches.
facts: Minor light and electric fog siren established fiscal year 1915 (PRIMARY: Commissioner of Lighthouses FY1915 report, p.8, as for Point Stuart). Upgraded to a separately manned Coast Guard light station in the late 1950s: keeper roster begins c.1957, new watch room 1960, four quarters completed 1961 - 'the last manned lighthouse built in California' (lighthousefriends, citing Shanks 1990; USCG July 1970 press release).

1915: unwatched lens-lantern light and siren on the island's southeast point, tended from Point Knox. c.1957-61: modern station - flat-roofed signal building with lens lantern and horn, watch building commanding the whole central bay, four ranch-style dwellings; absorbed control of Southampton Shoal and Raccoon Strait aids when Angel Island (Point Knox) station closed (USCG press release; lighthousefriends).
Lens lantern (1915); modern optic Fl G 5s with horn (Light List 2025).

To mark the southeastern corner of Angel Island where the main channels toward the river ports converge; the 1915 aid completed the island's triangle of lights (FY1915 report; USCG press release: guidance into the lanes toward the Sacramento and San Joaquin).

June 28, 1976 - 'the light would be automated and resident personnel would no longer be in attendance' (lighthousefriends, quoting the automation notice; the last manned lighthouse BUILT in California, though Point Bonita kept its keepers five years longer).
Station buildings remain in USCG hands on state-park island; closed to the public (lighthousefriends).
